Thomas Lancaster
lan'kas-ter
n. (d. 1584; Bishop of Kildare under Edward VI, deprived under Mary, and Archbishop of Armagh from 1568)
Lancaster, an English surname from the city on the Lune; Lune, the river, and Old English caster, from Latin castrum, a fort.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Thomas Lancaster was an Englishman and a convinced Protestant whose career tracks the whole of the Tudor religious reversal. Made Bishop of Kildare in 1549, he was consecrated by the new English ordinal, pressed the Prayer Book, married, and was deprived under Mary in 1554 for both his doctrine and his wife. He spent the Marian years in exile and in English parishes, returned under Elizabeth, and in 1568 was appointed Archbishop of Armagh, which he held until his death in 1584. He was one of the few archbishops of the period who actually tried to get preaching into the Irish parishes, repeatedly reporting to Dublin and London that there were neither ministers nor churches nor funds, and getting very little. The dictionary records him for the pattern of a ministry conducted across reversals: “But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry” (2Ti 4:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to deprive as to divest of an office or dignity; an evangelist as a preacher of the gospel, one who declares good tidings; and reproach as censure mingled with contempt, shame.

expand to see more

DEPRIVE, v.t. [L. deprivo.] To take from; to hinder from possessing or enjoying; to divest of an ecclesiastical preferment or office.

EVANGELIST, n. [Gr. euaggelistes.] A writer of the history of Jesus Christ; a preacher of the gospel; one who declares good tidings.

REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; abuse; shame; infamy; that which is the cause of shame.

ORDINAL, n. A book containing the order of divine service, especially the form of making and consecrating ministers.

PARTAKER, n. One who has or takes a part, share or portion in common with others.

Key Scripture

2Ti 4:5 — "But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry."

2Ti 1:8 — "Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God;"

Heb 13:13 — "Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach."

Act 5:41 — "And they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name."

Modern Corruption

Bishop of Kildare from 1549, deprived under Mary for his doctrine and his marriage, and Archbishop of Armagh from 1568 to 1584, pressing fruitlessly for preaching in the Irish parishes.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a flattening of the Tudor bishops worth refusing, which treats them all as weathervanes who turned with each reign. Many did. Lancaster did not: he was deprived, exiled and restored, and his doctrine in 1568 was his doctrine of 1549. The dictionary notes the distinction because it matters for how the Irish failure is explained. Armagh under Lancaster was not a see in the hands of a trimmer; it was a see in the hands of a reformer with no money, no clergy and no Irish.

The principle to recover is that endurance across reversals is part of the charge rather than an interruption of it. Paul's last charge to Timothy puts affliction inside the job description: “But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry” (2Ti 4:5), and the shame attached to it is to be owned rather than avoided — “Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner” (2Ti 1:8). Hebrews calls the reader outside the camp to bear reproach with Christ (Heb 13:13), and the apostles treat that reproach as an honour conferred (Act 5:41).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kakopatheo (G2553), to endure hardship; Greek oneidismos (G3680), reproach.

Greek kakopatheo (G2553) — to suffer evil, to endure affliction; 2 Timothy 4:5.

Greek euaggelistes (G2099) — an evangelist, a bringer of good news; 2 Timothy 4:5.

Greek plerophoreo (G4135) — to carry out fully, to make full proof; 2 Timothy 4:5.

Greek sugkakopatheo (G4777) — to suffer hardship along with; 2 Timothy 1:8.

Greek oneidismos (G3680) — reproach, reviling; Hebrews 13:13.

Usage

"“make full proof of thy ministry” (2Ti 4:5) — Bishop of Kildare 1549, deprived 1554, Archbishop of Armagh 1568."

"“Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord” (2Ti 1:8) — deprived for his doctrine and for his marriage."

"“rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name” (Act 5:41) — his doctrine in 1568 was his doctrine of 1549."
